frase_gancho.texto: A fossil bone turned into a face more than twelve thousand years ago.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the ingenuity of the artist, we move on to the ingenuity of the craftsman. In the last display case of the hall, you will see the weapons used to hunt the giants: stone points so finely carved that they look like jewels.

guion_corto.texto: This piece looks like a simple bone, but it is one of the oldest works of art in the Americas. It is called the Sacro de Tequixquiac, and it was carved between twelve thousand and fourteen thousand years ago. The bone is the sacrum, the part of the pelvis where the spine ends, of an extinct camelid, a relative of the llamas. Someone took advantage of its natural holes and retouched them with stone to form eyes, a nose, and a long snout: the head of an animal that many identify as a coyote. We do not know who made it or why. But one thing is astonishing: more than twelve thousand years ago, in the Valley of Mexico, someone looked at a bone and saw a face.

guion_largo.texto:
The workers who in 1870 were digging a canal to drain the Valley of Mexico, in the area of Tequixquiac, did not know they were about to bring a treasure to light. Among the remains of Ice Age animals, a bone with a strange appearance turned up: it seemed to have a face. Mexican naturalists studied it very soon afterward, and tradition mentions Mariano Bárcena among the first. Since then, it has never stopped intriguing those who see it.

Look first at the material. It is a sacrum, the triangular bone where the spinal column ends. The word “sacrum” comes from “sacred”: since antiquity it has been called the sacred bone. And it belonged to an extinct camelid, a relative of llamas and camels. Here is a surprising fact: camels were born in the Americas. Their ancestors evolved in North America and from there spread to Asia and South America, which is where llamas and camels come from. Thirteen thousand years ago they still lived in these lands, and the animal that gave this bone walked through the Valley of Mexico.

Now look at the carving. With stone tools, the artist widened the natural holes in the bone to mark the eyes, wore down the edge to suggest the ears, and cut away the end to form the snout. The artist added almost nothing: they read the shape the bone already had and completed it. It is a sculpture made by discovery, not by invention. Some see a coyote; others, a dog or a peccary. That uncertainty is not a flaw: it is part of the beauty of such an ancient image.

Why does it matter so much? Because for a long time it was thought that the first inhabitants of the Americas were newcomers, busy only with surviving. This piece says something else: there was time, and desire, to make something that was of no use for eating or hunting, only for meaning. That is to say: symbolic thought, art. Even so, its exact date is still debated, and scientists urge caution. But even with the most cautious margins, it would still be among the oldest works of art on the continent. In Europe, during those same millennia, bison were being painted in the caves of Altamira and Lascaux. Tequixquiac reminds us that in the Americas, too, there were people who looked at the world with an artist’s eyes.

And here is a detail for your tour. The coyote is an animal with a very long career in the Mesoamerican imagination. Further ahead, in the Toltec Hall, you will see a frieze where jaguars and coyotes follow one another, and a [warrior with a coyote helmet](mna_s05_guerrero_coyote). The great poet king of Texcoco was named Nezahualcóyotl, “hungry coyote.” And an old, mischievous deity, Huehuecóyotl, protected music and dance. Perhaps it all began with this bone head.

One last thought. Seeing faces where there are none, in a cloud, in a damp stain, or in a bone, is a very human impulse, and psychologists call it pareidolia. It is possible that whoever carved this piece more than twelve thousand years ago felt the same way: they looked at the bone, saw a face, and simply helped it appear.

texto: Find the holes in the bone that were retouched to form the eyes
Follow the edge of the bone: it suggests the ears and the snout
Imagine the animal that gave the bone: a Pleistocene camelid related to llamas

texto.Culture: Hunter-gatherers of the Lithic Stage (Upper Pleistocene)
texto.Material: Fossilized sacrum bone of an extinct camelid (Camelops)

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Sacro de Tequixquiac is a colonial sculpture carved from a cow bone.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a prehistoric work, carved on the fossilized sacrum of an extinct camelid between twelve thousand and fourteen thousand years ago.
